hints: Recall the seven SI base quantities: length, mass, time, electric current, temperature, amount of substance and luminous intensity, and check which list items match this set.
teacher_walkthrough: SI base quantities are the seven independent quantities defined by the SI system from which all other derived quantities are formed.
Electric current with unit ampere $A$ is an SI base quantity. Time with unit second $s$ is an SI base quantity.
Charge with unit coulomb $C$ is derived as $Q = It$. Force with unit newton $N$ is derived as $F = ma$.
Therefore underline electric current and time only.
walkthrough: B1: only electric current and time underlined, no others underlined.
common_pitfalls: Underlining charge because coulomb looks fundamental, but charge is derived from current multiplied by time.
Underlining force because it appears in $F = ma$, but force is a derived quantity with unit $kg\,m\,s^{-2}$.
Underlining only one of the two correct quantities, which loses the mark as both are required.

hints: Compare the given $s = \frac{1}{2}at^{2}$ with the full equation of motion $s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^{2}$ and identify what must be true about $u$ for the first term to vanish.
Recall the derivation of SUVAT equations assumes a particular behaviour of $a$ with time and a straight line path with no change in direction.
teacher_walkthrough: The full equation for displacement with constant acceleration is $$s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^{2}$$ where $u$ is initial velocity.
The given form $$s = \frac{1}{2}at^{2}$$ has no $ut$ term, so $u = 0$. Hence the object starts from rest with zero initial speed or velocity.
SUVAT equations also require acceleration $a$ to be uniform or constant in magnitude throughout time $t$, with motion in a straight line.
walkthrough: B1: initial speed or velocity is zero or object starts from rest.
B1: acceleration is constant or uniform in magnitude and in a straight line.
common_pitfalls: Stating only that velocity is constant, which contradicts the presence of acceleration $a$ in the formula.
Omitting the starting from rest condition and stating only uniform acceleration, which gives only one of the two marks.

formulas_used: a = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} = \text{gradient of } v\text{-}t \text{ graph}
hints: Recall acceleration is the gradient of a velocity-time graph, so compare the steepness of the line segments containing $t = 8.0\,s$ and $t = 14.0\,s$ to judge relative magnitude.
Recall a positive gradient means acceleration in the positive velocity direction and a negative gradient means acceleration in the opposite direction, then check the sign of the slope at each time.
teacher_walkthrough: Acceleration equals the gradient of the $v$ against $t$ graph: $$a = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}$$
At $t = 8.0\,s$ the graph has a shallow positive slope from $t = 0$ to $t = 12.0\,s$. At $t = 14.0\,s$ the graph has a steeper negative slope from $t = 12.0\,s$ to $t = 16.0\,s$.
Steeper gradient magnitude means larger acceleration magnitude, so magnitude at $t = 8.0\,s$ is less than magnitude at $t = 14.0\,s$.
Positive gradient at $t = 8.0\,s$ and negative gradient at $t = 14.0\,s$ mean the directions are opposite to each other.
walkthrough: B1: magnitude of acceleration at $t = 8.0\,s$ is less than that at $t = 14.0\,s$.
B1: direction at $t = 8.0\,s$ is opposite to direction at $t = 14.0\,s$.
common_pitfalls: Confusing velocity direction with acceleration direction, for example claiming acceleration is negative at $t = 8.0\,s$ because part of the velocity is negative.
Comparing velocities at the two times instead of comparing gradients, so commenting on speed rather than acceleration.

hints: Recall acceleration at $t = 4.0\,s$ is the gradient of the straight line section from $t = 0$ to $t = 12.0\,s$, so read two velocity values on this line.
Set up $a = (v - u)/t$ using the change in $v$ over the corresponding change in $t$, keeping the sign of the initial negative velocity correct.
teacher_walkthrough: Acceleration is the gradient of the $v$ against $t$ graph: $$a = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}$$
Magnitude is $2.5\,m\,s^{-2}$.
walkthrough: C1: $a =$ gradient or $a = (v-u)/t$ or $a = \Delta v / \Delta t$.
common_pitfalls: Ignoring the negative sign of the starting velocity and using $\Delta v = 20 - 10 = 10$ instead of $20 - (-10) = 30$.
Reading the small grid squares incorrectly, for example taking $v = -10\,m\,s^{-1}$ as $-8\,m\,s^{-1}$.

hints: Recall displacement is the signed area under the velocity-time graph from $t = 0$ to $t = 12.0\,s$, with area below the time axis negative and area above positive.
Split the area at $t = 4.0\,s$ where $v = 0$ into a negative triangle from 0 to 4.0 s and a positive triangle from 4.0 s to 12.0 s, then set up net area as positive minus negative.
teacher_walkthrough: Displacement equals the net signed area under the $v$ against $t$ graph: $$s = \text{area above axis} - \text{area below axis}$$
Area below axis from $t = 0$ to $t = 4.0\,s$: base $= 4.0 - 0 = 4.0\,s$, height $= 10\,m\,s^{-1}$. $$A_{1} = \frac{1}{2} \times 4.0 \times 10 = 2.0 \times 10 = 20\,m$$
Net displacement: $$s = A_{2} - A_{1} = 80 - 20 = 60\,m$$
Magnitude of displacement from X is $60\,m$.
walkthrough: C1: displacement $= [\frac{1}{2} \times (12-4) \times 20] - [\frac{1}{2} \times 4 \times 10]$ or equivalent SUVAT or trapezium method.
common_pitfalls: Adding the two triangle areas to get $100\,m$ by treating distance below the axis as positive distance instead of negative displacement.
Using total distance formula $s = \frac{1}{2}at^{2}$ with $a = 2.5\,m\,s^{-2}$ but forgetting the non-zero initial velocity $u = -10\,m\,s^{-1}$ at $t = 0$.
